value.overview: The Orchard Oriole is a small, slender songbird of the blackbird family. It breeds mainly in open, leafy habitats across much of the eastern and central United States and northern Mexico, then migrates south for the nonbreeding season. Males are chestnut and black, while females and young birds are yellowish-green. Although named for orchards, the species also uses river edges, woodland margins, farms, parks, plantations, and lightly wooded tropical habitats.
value.classification: The Orchard Oriole belongs to the family Icteridae, the New World blackbirds and orioles. Its scientific name is Icterus spurius.
value.identification: Adult males have a black head, back, throat, and upper chest, with rich chestnut underparts, shoulder patches, and rump. Females are yellow-green overall, with darker wings, pale wing bars, and a grayish or olive back. Immature males gradually develop the adult pattern and may show mixed yellow, green, chestnut, and black plumage. The species is smaller and slimmer than the Baltimore Oriole. Its song is a varied, hurried series of whistles and rattling notes.
value.rangeHabitat: The Orchard Oriole breeds from the Great Plains and eastern United States south into northern Mexico. During the nonbreeding season it occupies Mexico, Central America, and parts of northern South America. In Costa Rica it occurs as a migratory visitor, mainly during the northern winter, rather than as a resident or breeding species. It can be found in open woodland, forest edges, river margins, farms, gardens, parks, shade-coffee plantations, orchards, and other lightly wooded areas, generally avoiding dense continuous forest.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Orchard Orioles leave their North American breeding grounds from mid-summer into autumn and spend the northern winter in Mexico, Central America, and northern South America. In Costa Rica, they are primarily present during the nonbreeding season, with some individuals also recorded during migration.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place mainly from late spring through summer in open habitats containing scattered trees. The female usually weaves a suspended pouch from grasses and plant fibers, attaching it to a forked twig away from the trunk. A clutch commonly contains four to six pale blue or grayish eggs marked with darker spots. Incubation lasts about 12 to 14 days, and the species usually raises one brood, sometimes two, during a breeding season.
value.dietFeeding: Orchard Orioles eat mostly insects and other arthropods during the breeding season, including caterpillars, beetles, grasshoppers, ants, wasps, bugs, and spiders. They glean prey from leaves and twigs. Nectar, flowers, berries, and other fruit become increasingly important during migration and winter. In Costa Rica, they may feed in flowering trees, fruiting plants, forest edges, plantations, gardens, and other habitats offering both insects and plant foods.
value.behavior: This species usually forages in trees and shrubs, often moving actively through foliage. It is relatively less territorial than many breeding songbirds, and several pairs may nest near one another where habitat is favorable. Males sing from exposed perches and use postures such as bowing and wing movements during courtship. On the wintering grounds, Orchard Orioles may forage in loose groups and join communal roosts with other birds.

conservation.populationTrend: The North American breeding population has declined substantially since the late twentieth century, despite increases or stability in some regions.
conservation.threats: Loss and degradation of open woodland, river-edge vegetation, orchards, and other breeding habitats can reduce nesting opportunities. Grazing and alteration of riverside habitats may also remove shrubs and increase nest parasitism by cowbirds. Because the species migrates between countries, habitat quality on both breeding and wintering grounds is important.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore open woodland, riparian vegetation, hedgerows, orchards, and shade-grown agricultural habitats. Retain mature and scattered trees, native shrubs, and flowering or fruiting plants. Reduce unnecessary pesticide use and support conservation of migratory bird habitat in North America, Central America, and northern South America.
